history.summary:

One of the oldest and most powerful of the 51 Shakti Peethas, the Kamakhya Temple stands atop Nilachal Hill in Guwahati - the spot where, per legend, Sati's yoni fell as Lord Shiva carried her corpse and Lord Vishnu's Sudarshana Chakra dismembered it. The sanctum has no idol: devotees worship a yoni-shaped rock formation bathed by an underground spring, symbol of creative feminine energy, and the temple is India's premier centre of Shaktism and Tantric worship. The earliest temple was destroyed by Muslim invaders in the early 16th century; the current beehive-shikhara structure was built in 1565-66 by Koch King Nara Narayana, with later contributions from Ahom kings. The Ambubachi Mela (June) celebrates the goddess's annual menstruation - the sanctum stays closed for three days (verify dates yearly) and reopens on the fourth to huge crowds. General darshan is free; special/VIP darshan passes (Rs 501) reduce waits of several hours.

town_description: Guwahati is the largest city of Northeast India, spread along the south bank of the Brahmaputra river in Kamrup Metropolitan district; Dispur, the capital of Assam, is its eastern suburb. Known as the 'City of Temples', it hosts Kamakhya, Umananda, Navagraha, Sukreswar and other historic shrines, plus the IIT Guwahati campus across the river. It is the gateway to the Northeast, well connected by air, rail and road.

travel.airport: Lokpriya Gopinath Bordoloi International Airport - about 20 km (45-60 min).
travel.railway: Kamakhya Junction - about 6-8 km; Guwahati Railway Station - about 8 km; city buses and taxis to the Nilachal hill base, then steps or vehicle to the temple.
travel.road: Guwahati is well connected by NH-27 and other highways; ASTC buses run to Guwahati city, with local buses/taxis up Nilachal Hill (verify routes).

visitor_information.best_time: October to March; early morning (6:00-8:00 AM weekdays) for the shortest queues; avoid the Ambubachi Mela week unless visiting for the mela.
visitor_information.opening_hours: General darshan 8:00 AM-1:00 PM and 2:30-5:30 PM; temple opens ~5:30 AM for priestly rites (snana/nitya puja) and closes to devotees ~5:30 PM after evening aarti; closed 1:00-2:30 PM. Exact session boundaries vary across sources (verify).
